summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
Per the U.S. GAO, twenty of 23 major federal agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, with NASA and the Department of Commerce reporting the highest number. Three agencies reported having no uses for AI. Most of the reported use cases were still in the planning phase rather than in production, and in about 200 instances agencies said they were currently using AI. The GAO found that only five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their reported use cases, while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, and two inventories included uses later determined not to be AI.

What agencies actually deploy AI for, per the GAO, includes analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, identifying information security threats, and facilitating the review of large datasets. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. The GAO notes that the Office of Management and Budget has not yet developed government-wide guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, and the Office of Personnel Management has not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work.

On the state side, theworldofai.org tracks 5,934 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan. Its review of 100 measures across 27 states, completed on September 18, 2026, found that no two states wrote the same law. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors: Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149. Every other measure names one setting, such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom, or a state agency. The recurring rule where stakes are personal is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider: insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions.

Enforcement is concentrated. Per theworldofai.org, no state in the reviewed set created a new agency to enforce AI law. The attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act. A private right to sue is the exception, appearing mainly where one identifiable person is harmed. The site's synthesis for businesses is to build to the common core: tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits, or education, have a crisis protocol and know the age of the user if the product holds a conversation, and keep records of what the system does.

Stanford HAI's AI Index frames the broader problem as a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, noting that frameworks to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology are falling behind while data transparency declines. OECD.AI gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives and tracks work under the OECD AI Principles, with the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' AI work joined under the GPAI brand in July 2024. Oxford Insights runs the Government AI Readiness Index, scoring countries on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption, and works directly with governments to change how services are delivered.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy AI in a government context, the record shows a field where adoption is real but uneven, inventories are unreliable, and federal acquisition guidance is still missing. The state patchwork means the question is never whether you use AI, per theworldofai.org, but what you use it for, and the attorney general is the enforcer you are most likely to meet. The GAO's finding that most federal use cases are still in planning, combined with incomplete inventories, suggests that the management layer, not the technology, is the binding constraint.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports tracking 5,932 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan, and compares 100 enacted measures across 27 states as of September 18, 2026. It notes that no two states wrote the same law, and only Colorado and Texas passed broad laws covering consequential decisions across sectors, while other measures target specific settings. A recurring rule is that AI may assist but cannot be the sole decider in personal matters, such as insurers denying care on an algorithm alone or AI delivering therapy. The page states no state created a new enforcement agency; attorneys general enforce the larger laws, and some states treat violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices. It advises building to common duties like disclosing AI use, keeping a qualified person in health, employment, benefits, or education decisions, and keeping records because the attorney general is the most likely enforcer.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
